trial_name: CLOVERS — Early Restrictive or Liberal Fluid Management for Sepsis-Induced Hypotension (2023)
citation: Shapiro NI, Douglas IS, Brower RG, Brown SM, Exline MC, Ginde AA, et al. Early restrictive or liberal fluid management for sepsis-induced hypotension. N Engl J Med. 2023;388:499-510.
one_liner: In adults with sepsis-induced hypotension after 1–3 L crystalloid, an early restrictive fluid/vasopressor-prioritised strategy did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with a liberal fluid strategy (13.9% vs 14.9%, risk difference −0.9 pp, 95% CI −4.4 to 2.6).

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) with suspected/confirmed infection and sepsis-induced hypotension after receiving 1–3 L crystalloid, SBP <100 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg or already on vasopressors.
pico.intervention: Restrictive fluid strategy: prioritise early norepinephrine to target MAP ≥65 mmHg, minimal additional crystalloid during 24-hour protocol; fluid boluses only as rescue for severe hypotension or hypoperfusion non-responsive to vasopressors; peripheral vasopressor allowed.
pico.comparison: Liberal fluid strategy: prioritise additional isotonic crystalloid boluses (initial 2 L over 24 h, later amended to optional second litre) before vasopressors; vasopressors reserved for persistent hypotension or fluid overload concerns.
pico.outcome: Death before discharge home by day 90 (primary); all-cause mortality, ventilator-free days, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, ICU-free days, hospital-free days, initiation of mechanical ventilation/RRT, ARDS, serious adverse events.

background.existing_knowledge: Adult sepsis guidance has historically promoted early intravenous crystalloids (commonly 30 mL/kg within first hours), despite low/very low-certainty evidence and concerns about fluid accumulation and organ oedema.
background.knowledge_gap: Clinicians face an early “after 1–3 L” decision: continue fluids to augment preload vs initiate vasopressors. Adjacent trials (CLASSIC, FRESH, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK) left the early hypotension decision unresolved.
background.hypothesis: An early restrictive fluid strategy (prioritising earlier vasopressors and less crystalloid) would improve 90-day outcomes vs liberal strategy.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, open-label, pragmatic superiority trial with protocolised 24-hour treatment guidance, stratified by site.
methods.setting: 60 US centres (predominantly emergency department; randomisation within 4 hours, median 61 min).

inclusion: Adults ≥18 years with suspected/confirmed infection and sepsis-induced hypotension
Received 1–3 L intravenous isotonic crystalloid pre-randomisation
SBP <100 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg after initial fluids, or already receiving vasopressors
exclusion: Clinician-determined need for immediate alternative management
Overt pulmonary oedema / severe volume overload precluding protocolised fluid restriction

methods.intervention: Restrictive: early norepinephrine (MAP ≥65 mmHg), minimal additional crystalloid (median 500 mL in first 6 h); fluid boluses only for prespecified rescue indications; peripheral vasopressor initiation allowed.
methods.comparison: Liberal: prioritised additional crystalloid boluses (initial 2 L, later amended optional second litre); vasopressors reserved for persistent hypotension or fluid overload.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned n=2320 to detect 4.5% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (15% to 10.5%) at 90% power, α 0.05; stopped early at 1563 for futility.
methods.primary_outcome: Death before discharge home by day 90
secondary_outcomes: Initiation of mechanical ventilation by day 28
Initiation of renal-replacement therapy by day 28
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint through day 90; organ-support–free days assessed at day 28; complications to day 7.

headline_bullets: Stopped early for futility at 1563 patients; no difference in primary outcome (13.9% restrictive vs 14.9% liberal, risk diff −0.9 pp, 95% CI −4.4 to 2.6, p=0.61).
All secondary mortality and organ-support endpoints neutral; all-location 90-day mortality 22.4% vs 21.9% (diff 0.5 pp, CI −3.6 to 4.7).
Restrictive strategy reduced 24-hour fluid by ~2.1 L (median 3300 vs 5400 mL) but increased vasopressor use (59% vs 37%), earlier initiation, and central/peripheral line insertion.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death before discharge home by day 90 (primary)
Death from any cause at any location by day 90

outcomes_table.note: Numerically fewer vasopressor-free days in restrictive arm (expected direction)

outcomes_table.outcome: Initiation of mechanical ventilation by day 28
Initiation of renal-replacement therapy by day 28
Total crystalloid from pre-enrolment through 24 h (median, IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Crystalloid in first 6 h: median 500 mL (IQR 0–1000) vs 2300 mL (IQR 1600–3000)
Median time to vasopressor: 2.4 vs 3.9 h (diff −1.4 h, CI −1.8 to −1.1); mean duration: 14.4 vs 10.2 h (diff 4.2 h, CI 2.5 to 5.9)

outcomes_table.outcome: Central venous catheter insertion (randomisation to 72 h)
outcomes_table.note: Peripheral vasopressor use: 36.9% vs 27.4% (diff 9.5 pp, CI 5.0 to 14.0)

safety: Fluid overload/pulmonary oedema: 0 events (restrictive) vs 3 events (liberal).
Serious adverse events: 21 vs 19 events (difference 2, 95% CI −10 to 14).

domains.notes: Centralised randomisation stratified by institution; allocation concealment feasible; unblinded by design.
Open-label delivery could influence co-interventions and discharge decisions; primary endpoint mortality-based, objective, but secondary endpoints (ICU/hospital days) susceptible.
1563 randomised, primary endpoint status largely complete; censoring rare (0.6% vs 0.5%). Intention-to-treat analysis maintained.

Protocol guidance used in 97.3% restrictive vs 96.0% liberal; substantial treatment separation achieved (fluids, vasopressor timing). Rescue actions permitted, some bidirectional contamination expected but limited.
Groups well balanced: mean age ~62 years, median pre-randomisation crystalloid 2050 mL both arms, mean lactate 2.9 mmol/L both arms. Early stopping did not introduce imbalance.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity moderate-to-strong: randomisation and protocol fidelity robust with clear treatment separation, primary endpoint objective; open-label performance bias on secondary endpoints and reduced precision from early stopping are principal threats.

domains.notes: Enrolled a broad emergency-care sepsis-induced hypotension population after initial crystalloid (median 2050 mL) with moderate severity (mean lactate 2.9 mmol/L); excluded patients who had already received >3 L crystalloid or had overt fluid overload.
60 US centres with vasopressor and monitoring capabilities; generalisability lower in low-resource settings where peripheral vasopressor initiation may be less feasible or monitoring insufficient.

external_validity.verdict: Highly generalisable to high-income emergency and early critical care settings managing sepsis-induced hypotension after initial crystalloid, but less applicable to extreme shock phenotypes, late resuscitation after very large fluid volumes, and resource-limited contexts.

strengths: Early randomisation within clinically relevant decision window
Substantial treatment separation (fluid volume, vasopressor timing)
Patient-important 90-day endpoint with complementary all-location mortality
Detailed supplementary reporting on protocol epochs and vascular access consequences
limitations: Open-label strategy trial (risk of performance effects on ICU/hospital utilisation outcomes)
Early stopping for futility reduced precision for modest effect sizes
Intervention bundled multiple linked decisions (fluid volume, vasopressor timing, line strategy), limiting mechanistic attribution
Liberal arm protocol amendment mid-trial reflects real-world practice but complicates a “single fixed-dose” interpretation

critical_appraisal.summary: CLOVERS is a well-conducted, pragmatic strategy trial with robust treatment separation and a neutral outcome; internal validity is moderate (open-label, early stopping) but external validity is high; the tight confidence intervals exclude large benefit for either strategy, supporting individualised resuscitation.

sections.authors_conclusion: An early vasopressor-prioritised, fluid-restrictive approach after the first 1–3 L is a defensible alternative to continued liberal fluids in sepsis-induced hypotension, as neither strategy improved 90-day mortality; choice should be individualised to phenotype (fluid responsiveness, cardiac/renal reserve, pulmonary oedema risk, and perfusion markers).

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: CLOVERS does not mandate a single resuscitation strategy; it demonstrates that both an early vasopressor/restrictive fluid approach and a liberal fluid approach yield similar 90-day outcomes, allowing clinicians to tailor based on patient physiology.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with sepsis-induced hypotension who have received 1–3 L crystalloid and remain hypotensive, in high-income emergency/critical care settings.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not justify withholding initial crystalloid in sepsis or adopting a blanket restrictive approach for all patients. It also does not prove that early vasopressors are superior.
implementation_caveats: Restrictive strategy increases vasopressor exposure and invasive line use, potentially shifting resource burden.
Peripheral vasopressor initiation requires monitoring protocols and training.
Fluid responsiveness assessment may help guide individual decisions.

controversies.notes: Primary endpoint embeds discharge destination; near-identical all-location 90-day mortality confirms no mortality signal, mitigating concern about artefact.
Stopping early improved efficiency but reduced precision; the primary outcome CI (−4.4 to 2.6 pp) leaves residual uncertainty about modest benefit/harm.
Amendment from mandatory 2 L to optional second litre did not alter mortality effect (epoch interaction p=0.855), supporting stability of neutral conclusion.
CLASSIC (ICU-phase restrictive vs liberal in septic shock) also showed neutral mortality, reinforcing that restrictive fluid is not automatically superior across phases.

Contemporary guidance increasingly emphasises individualised fluid resuscitation, dynamic assessment, and early vasopressors when appropriate; recent ESICM recommendations separate fluid choice from volume decisions.
Systematic reviews show no consistent large mortality advantage of higher vs lower resuscitation volumes; vasopressor timing may be modifiable but confounded.

context_related_trials.relation: ICU-phase restrictive vs liberal fluid in septic shock; also neutral mortality, supporting lack of superiority of restrictive approach.
Physiology-guided resuscitation using dynamic assessments; analogous approach but different decision trigger.
Targeted perfusion pressure vs lactate clearance; also influenced vasopressor use patterns.

unresolved_questions: Are there subgroups (e.g., truly fluid-responsive patients, those with renal insufficiency) that benefit from one strategy over the other?
What is the optimal method to identify fluid responsiveness early?
How to safely implement peripheral vasopressors in various settings?
Does very early vasopressor initiation (≤1 L crystalloid) improve outcomes?
What is the role of balanced crystalloids vs saline in this context?

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: 13.9% vs 14.9% (risk diff −0.9 pp, 95% CI −4.4 to 2.6)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In sepsis-induced hypotension after 1–3 L crystalloid, neither earlier vasopressors (restrictive) nor additional fluids (liberal) is superior for 90-day mortality, supporting individualised resuscitation.
